---
title: "Quickstart"
---

Choose a NaN policy, inspect boundary effects, and select a local statistic.
These examples introduce the established [numerical semantics](guides/semantics.qmd)
using small arrays with no external data.

## 1. Install the source build

The first PyPI release is being prepared. Follow the current
[source-build instructions](https://github.com/ysBach/ndfiltrs#source-build),
including their Rust dependency requirements. The examples require a built
`ndfiltrs` extension and NumPy.

## 2. Decide how missing samples count

```python
import numpy as np
import ndfiltrs as nf

line = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 5.0])
plain = nf.median_filter(line, size=3)
omitted = nf.nanmedian_filter(line, size=3)

assert np.isnan(plain).all()
np.testing.assert_array_equal(omitted, [1.0, 3.0, 5.0])
omitted
# array([1., 3., 5.])
```

The center median uses the two retained samples, `1` and `5`. With the
default `reflect` boundary, edge samples repeat and count separately.
Require more support when your analysis needs it:

```python
strict = nf.nanmedian_filter(line, size=3, min_count=3)
assert np.isnan(strict).all()
```

Set `ignore_inf=True` to omit infinities as well as NaNs. A finite hot pixel
still counts as valid; mark known bad pixels yourself.

## 3. Inspect the boundary rule

```python
finite = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 9.0])
reflected = nf.median_filter(finite, size=3, mode="reflect")
padded = nf.median_filter(finite, size=3, mode="constant", cval=0.0)

np.testing.assert_array_equal(reflected, [1.0, 2.0, 9.0])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(padded, [1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
```

At the right edge, reflection produces the window `[2, 9, 9]`; constant
padding produces `[2, 9, 0]`. Their medians differ because the boundary rule
changes the samples, even though the input array is identical.

## 4. Select a statistic

```python
local_mean = nf.mean_filter(finite, size=3)
local_median = nf.median_filter(finite, size=3)

assert local_mean[1] == 4.0
assert local_median[1] == 2.0
np.testing.assert_array_equal(finite, [1.0, 2.0, 9.0])
```

Both center windows contain `[1, 2, 9]`. The mean is `4`; the median is `2`.
Choose the statistic for the scientific quantity you intend to estimate.
These functions produce a filtered array without changing `finite`.
